lesson.title: Counting What Counts: Significant Figures in Measurement
lesson.summary: Significant figures are the digits in a measurement that carry real information, and clear rules for counting, rounding, and calculating with them keep a result from claiming more precision than the data actually supports.
lesson.body:
Every measurement you make with a real instrument, as the Measurement unit established, involves reading a scale and estimating one final digit that lies between the smallest marked divisions. Significant figures are the tool chemists use to keep track of exactly which digits in a recorded number are trustworthy and which ones are just noise. A meter stick marked in millimeters lets you read a length like 12.4 cm with confidence in the 12 and a reasonable estimate on the 4, but writing that same length as 12.40000 cm would falsely claim a level of precision the ruler never provided. Significant figures exist to prevent that kind of overstatement, and to make sure a calculated answer never appears more precise than the actual measurements that produced it.

Counting significant figures follows a short set of rules. All nonzero digits are always significant: 247 has three. Zeros trapped between nonzero digits are always significant: 1005 has four. Leading zeros, the ones that only mark the position of the decimal point, are never significant: 0.0034 has only two significant figures, the 3 and the 4. Trailing zeros are significant only when the number contains a decimal point, since that decimal point signals the zero was actually measured rather than just a placeholder: 3.00 has three significant figures, but 300 by itself is ambiguous and is usually assumed to have only one unless written in scientific notation as 3.00 x 10^2, which unambiguously shows three.

These rules become essential once measurements are combined in a calculation, because different operations propagate uncertainty differently. For multiplication and division, the answer keeps only as many significant figures as the measurement with the fewest. For addition and subtraction, the answer keeps only as many decimal places as the measurement with the fewest decimal places, since you cannot report a value more precisely than your least precise piece of data allowed. Consider a rectangular plate measured as 12.4 cm long and 0.30 cm wide. Multiplying gives 12.4 x 0.30 = 3.72 cm^2 on a calculator, but 0.30 has only two significant figures while 12.4 has three, so the reported area must be rounded to two significant figures: 3.7 cm^2. Now consider adding three masses measured on different balances: 12.11 g, 0.3 g, and 1.001 g. The raw sum is 13.411 g, but the 0.3 g measurement is only known to one decimal place, so the answer must be rounded to one decimal place: 13.4 g, even though that seems to throw away digits the more precise balances clearly measured.

This might feel like an arbitrary rule, but it reflects something real about how uncertainty spreads through a calculation. If the plate's width is only known to within 0.01 cm, no amount of precision in the length measurement can make the calculated area more certain than that width allows. Reporting 3.72 cm^2 would falsely claim a confidence in the third digit that the data does not support. Chemists take this seriously because errors compound: a measurement with fabricated precision fed into a stoichiometry calculation or a rate law produces a final answer that looks authoritative but is actually built on sand.

As you move into scientific notation and dimensional analysis, you will use significant figures constantly to check whether a converted or calculated value still reflects the real precision of the original data, and rounding correctly at each step, rather than only at the very end, is what keeps that precision honest all the way through a multi step problem.
